_comment: The ratio of valgebra to pydantic-core each shape must stay under: a claim the project makes, not a measurement it recorded. Ratios cancel a machine's absolute speed but not its interpreter or whether the wheel was PGO-built. The interpreter is the one that moves a shape far: on a single box a schema nested twenty-five deep takes 0.14 to 0.16 of pydantic's time under CPython 3.12 and 3.14 and 0.33 under the free-threaded build, because every read of an element out of a mutable container takes that container's lock there. So a recorded ratio is a number that must be re-recorded per environment, which is the failure this file exists not to repeat. The lane these are read on names its interpreter in ci.yml -- CPython 3.12 -- rather than taking whichever one the runner image ships, because a ratio belongs to the interpreter as much as to the two libraries. Each ceiling sits well above what the shape measures in both environments and well below the point where the claim would stop being true. Changing one is an edit with an argument in its commit message; scripts/perf_gate.py --against is the fine-grained gate. The ceilings were tightened once the shapes moved under them: a list of scalars stopped walking its elements through the general walk, a record stopped scanning the value it could ask for its keys, the failure path stopped copying the names it already held, and it stopped searching a value for a key it had already accounted for. A ceiling a shape passes by six times over is a claim about nothing, so each sits above what the shape measures in the *worse* of the two environments -- and which environment that is differs per shape, which is the trap this file exists to remember. Six of the seven read within a fifth of each other across the interpreters the lanes run, `large_array` among them once a list of one scalar kind stopped being read element by owned element: 0.19 under CPython 3.12, which the bench lane runs, against 0.15 under 3.14 and 0.16 free-threaded. Deep nesting is the shape that parts, and it has a set of its own below.
_free_threaded_comment: Ceilings the free-threaded build is held to instead, for the shapes where it is a different performance environment rather than the same one on a slower clock. A shape absent from here is held to the shared ceiling above. Reading an element out of a list takes the list's lock there, and a shape whose cost is per-element pays it: a schema nested twenty-five deep is twenty-five single-element lists, and it measures 0.309 to 0.338 of pydantic's time across four runs where the interpreters with a global lock read 0.142 to 0.162. The claim this project makes of that build is the true one, and the way to lower it is to stop owning an element the walk only reads.
_recorded_comment: Beside each ceiling -- what the project claims -- the ratio the shape last measured, and the spread it was measured across. A ceiling a shape passes by a wide margin stops measuring it: the JSON document sat at 0.87 under a ceiling of 1.00 while a commit message published 0.78 for it, and no gate was red for as long as it took somebody to re-run this one for an unrelated reason. The mutation ratchet and the instruction gate both compare against a recorded baseline; this is that, for ratios. A shape measuring worse than `ratios + tolerance` is red even while it is under its ceiling, and re-recording is an edit with an argument in its commit message, exactly as changing a ceiling is. The tolerance is the shape's own spread across runs of one build, measured per shape rather than assumed: one run cannot see it, so `--update` leaves it alone. A recorded ratio belongs to an environment as much as to the two libraries -- the interpreter, its global lock, and the pydantic-core it was compared against, since a faster pydantic-core raises every ratio with nothing here changing -- so the block names the environment it was taken in and the gate refuses to judge anywhere else, which is the failure the ceilings comment above already warns about once.

unratcheted.error_report: Not measurable on this instrument. Five runs of one PGO CPython 3.12 build read 0.861, 0.882, 0.889, 1.056 and 1.193 -- a spread of 0.33, a third of the shape's own value, where every other shape spreads between 0.001 and 0.048. A tolerance wide enough not to fire on that noise would be wider than any regression worth catching, and a tighter one would fire constantly. The shape keeps its ceiling of 1.60, which it is nowhere near crossing, and the reason it is noisy is worth its own reading: it is the only shape timing a path that raises and formats an exception, so a Python exception's cost is inside the measurement.

recorded._how_to_arm: Unrecorded on purpose. The fingerprint is the interpreter, its lock and the pydantic-core version, and a recording made elsewhere would match the bench lane's fingerprint while carrying another machine's noise -- which would arm the ratchet on numbers that were never taken there. So the first `--update` belongs on the lane, as a commit whose message carries the run it recorded. The tolerances below are not waiting for that: they are the shapes' own spread, measured over twelve runs of one PGO CPython 3.12 build -- scalar 0.008, large_array 0.004, deep_nesting 0.014, wide_record 0.029, json_document 0.057, build 0.001 -- each rounded up, and a spread is a property of the shape rather than of the box it was read on.
